title: The Man Who Invented Testing
hook: A thousand years ago, one scholar insisted that you must test an idea, not just argue it.
story: Ibn al-Haytham was born around 965 in Basra, in what is now Iraq, and spent most of his working life in Cairo. In his time the accepted account of vision came from ancient Greek authorities, and several of them held that the eye sends out rays which touch the world and feel it, rather like invisible fingers. It was quoted confidently because Ptolemy and Euclid had said so.

He refused to settle the question by citing an authority, which was the genuinely radical part. Instead he built a dark chamber with a small hole in one wall and watched an upside-down image of the outside world appear on the opposite wall. If the eye sent out rays, a room should not be able to see. He worked through lenses, mirrors, shadows and reflections, and concluded that light travels in straight lines from objects into the eye.

More important than any single result was how he worked. Do an experiment. Write down exactly what you did and what happened, so that someone else can repeat it and disagree. Treat your own conclusions as things to be attacked. He wrote that a seeker after truth should suspect the writings of others and question his own findings from every side, so that he does not fall into prejudice — which is close to a description of science three centuries before Europe assembled one.

His Book of Optics was translated into Latin and shaped European thinkers from Roger Bacon to Kepler. There is a story, impossible to verify, that he produced much of it while under house arrest in Cairo after promising the ruler he could dam the Nile and then realising the task was far beyond the engineering of the age. Whether or not that is true, he is one reason we now expect an idea to be tested rather than merely argued.
wow: He wrote much of his greatest work while under house arrest, after a plan of his to dam the Nile proved impossible.

quiz.q: What did Ibn al-Haytham show about vision?
What was his most important habit?
a: Testing ideas and recording the method

title: Marie Curie
hook: She discovered two elements, won two Nobel Prizes, and drove x-ray vans to the front line.
story: Maria Skłodowska grew up in Warsaw under Russian rule, where universities did not admit women and Polish learning was suppressed. She studied in secret at an underground night school, then worked as a governess for years while sending money to support her sister's studies in Paris, on the understanding that her sister would later support her. Both kept the bargain. She arrived in Paris at 24, lived in an unheated attic where ink froze in winter, and finished first in her physics class.

Working with her husband Pierre, she investigated the strange rays coming from uranium and made the crucial leap: the effect came from inside the atoms themselves, not from any chemical reaction. At the time atoms were thought to be indivisible and unchanging, so this was a genuine break with what everyone believed. Sifting through tonnes of a sticky black mineral waste in a leaking shed, the couple extracted two new elements — polonium, named for the homeland that did not officially exist, and radium.

She won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, and only after Pierre insisted that her name be added to the nomination. After he was killed by a horse-drawn wagon in 1906 she took over his professorship, the first woman to teach at the Sorbonne, and in 1911 won a second Nobel Prize, in Chemistry. She remains the only person to have won in two different sciences.

When war came in 1914 she did something intensely practical. Realising that wounded soldiers were dying because surgeons could not locate bullets and shattered bone, she raised money for mobile X-ray units, learned to drive and to repair the vehicles, trained women to operate them, and drove to the front herself with her teenage daughter. Over a million wounded men were examined. She died in 1934 of an illness almost certainly caused by her own work, and her notebooks are still radioactive.
wow: Her notebooks are still radioactive, and must be handled with protective clothing.

quiz.q: What was new about her finding?
a: The rays came from inside atoms

quiz.q: What did she do in the First World War?
a: Built and drove mobile x-ray units

title: Ada Lovelace
hook: She wrote instructions for a computer that had not been built yet.
story: Ada Byron was born in London in 1815, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, who left within weeks and never saw her again. Her mother, fearing that poetry had ruined the father, had her taught mathematics and logic intensively from early childhood — an unusual education for a girl of that period, and one designed to keep imagination in check. It did not work as intended.

At seventeen she met Charles Babbage, who was designing an enormous mechanical calculating machine of brass gears, cranks and punched cards called the Analytical Engine. It was never built in his lifetime — the engineering was at the limit of what Victorian workshops could manage, and funding collapsed — but the design was serious and complete.

In 1843 Ada translated an Italian article describing the machine, and added notes of her own. The notes ran three times longer than the article. In one, labelled Note G, she worked through exactly how the engine could be instructed, step by step, to calculate a difficult sequence of numbers, including how it would loop back and repeat operations. It is a program, written for a computer that did not exist, and it is why she is often called the first programmer.

She also saw something Babbage did not. He thought of his machine as a calculator for numbers. Ada argued that if any subject — music, letters, images — could be represented by symbols, then the engine could operate on those symbols too, and might one day compose elaborate pieces of music. That leap, from arithmetic to information in general, is essentially what a computer turned out to be. She also wrote, carefully, that the machine could originate nothing, and could only do what we know how to order it to perform — an argument people are still having about computers today. She died at 36.
wow: She also wrote that the machine could never truly originate anything, only do what we order it to perform — an argument people still debate about computers today.

quiz.q: What did Ada Lovelace write?
a: A program for a machine not yet built

quiz.q: What did she realise the machine could handle?
a: Anything that can be written as symbols

title: Alan Turing
hook: He imagined what a computer could be, then helped break a code that shortened a war.
story: In 1936, before any computer existed, Alan Turing published a paper describing an imaginary machine: an endless strip of tape, a head that could read and write symbols on it, and a simple table of rules. He proved that such a machine could carry out any calculation that can be described as a step-by-step procedure — and also, in the same paper, that some questions can never be answered by any machine at all, no matter how long it runs. Every computer built since has been a version of his idea.

During the Second World War he worked at Bletchley Park on German military codes. The Enigma machine scrambled messages differently every day, giving so many possible settings that testing them by hand was hopeless. Turing helped design an electro-mechanical machine that hunted instead for contradictions — assuming a setting, following the consequences, and discarding it the moment something impossible appeared. That let the team throw away billions of wrong answers quickly.

Decoded messages helped route Atlantic convoys around waiting submarines, and historians generally think the work shortened the war by around two years. It was also secret for decades, so almost nobody knew what he had done, and he could not put it on a curriculum vitae.

Britain treated him appallingly afterwards. In 1952 he reported a burglary, the investigation revealed a relationship with a man, and he was prosecuted for gross indecency — homosexuality was then a crime. He was given hormone treatment as an alternative to prison and stripped of his security clearance. He died in 1954, aged 41, from cyanide poisoning, generally recorded as suicide. An official government apology came in 2009 and a royal pardon in 2013. He had by then also proposed the question that still shapes arguments about artificial intelligence: if you cannot tell a machine's answers from a person's, on what grounds do you insist it does not think?
wow: He also proposed a test for machine intelligence: if you cannot tell a machine's answers from a person's, on what basis do you deny it thinks?

quiz.q: What did Turing describe in 1936?
a: An imaginary machine that could compute anything

quiz.q: What did his wartime work do?

title: Katherine Johnson
hook: An astronaut refused to fly until she had checked the computer's sums by hand.
story: Katherine Johnson was a mathematician at what became NASA, hired into a pool of women who worked out calculations by hand, with pencils and mechanical adding machines. Their job title was literally computer, because that is what the word meant before it meant a machine. Black staff were assigned to a segregated section, required to use separate facilities, and kept out of meetings.

She kept asking to attend the engineers' briefings where the work was actually decided. The standard answer was that women did not go. She asked whether there was a law against it, kept asking, and eventually they stopped objecting — a small, stubborn act repeated until it worked.

Her speciality was orbital mechanics: calculating the path a spacecraft must follow to leave the Earth, arrive where it is meant to, and come down in the right stretch of ocean. She worked out the trajectory for Alan Shepard's flight in 1961, the first American in space, which had to be precise because the capsule could not steer itself.

In 1962, before John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth, NASA had switched to electronic computers — and nobody entirely trusted them yet. Glenn asked engineers to have the girl check the numbers, meaning Johnson specifically, and said that if she confirmed them he was ready to go. She spent days working through the machine's output by hand. The numbers matched. He flew. She went on to work on the Apollo Moon landings, including calculations for the flight that carried Armstrong and Aldrin, and on the rescue of Apollo 13. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015, aged 97, and died at 101.
wow: She received America's highest civilian honour in 2015, aged 97, and lived to 101.

quiz.q: What did Katherine Johnson calculate?
Why did John Glenn ask for her?
a: He wanted her to check the computer

title: Jane Goodall
hook: She watched chimpanzees make tools, and forced science to redefine what a human is.
story: Jane Goodall arrived at Gombe in what is now Tanzania in 1960, aged 26, to study wild chimpanzees. She had no university degree, which many scientists held against her, and she had been chosen partly for that reason: the palaeontologist Louis Leakey wanted an observer whose mind had not been shaped by existing theory. Colonial officials refused to let a young woman live alone in the bush, so her mother came with her for the first months.

She worked differently from the accepted method. She sat still for weeks until the chimpanzees stopped fleeing, and she gave them names — David Greybeard, Flo, Fifi — rather than numbers, which was criticised as sentimental and unscientific. It turned out to reveal something real: chimpanzees have distinct, lasting personalities, and treating them as interchangeable specimens hides that.

Then, in her first year, she watched David Greybeard pick a twig, strip the leaves from it, push it into a termite mound and pull it out covered in termites to eat. He had not found a tool. He had made one, modifying an object for a purpose. At the time, toolmaking was widely used as the line separating humans from animals. Leakey wrote back that science must now either redefine tool, redefine man, or accept chimpanzees as human.

She kept recording things people did not want to hear: chimpanzees hunting and eating monkeys, comforting each other after conflict, adopting orphans, and — over four grim years in the 1970s — systematically killing members of a neighbouring group in what looked uncomfortably like war. She later left fieldwork for campaigning, spending decades travelling to argue for conservation, and was still speaking publicly into her nineties.
wow: She was still travelling and speaking about conservation into her nineties.

quiz.q: What did she see David Greybeard do?
a: Make a tool from a twig
Use a stone as a hammer

quiz.q: Why was that important?
a: Toolmaking was thought to be uniquely human
Chimps were thought to eat only fruit

title: Srinivasa Ramanujan
hook: A clerk in Madras posted strange formulas to a Cambridge professor. Most of them were right.
story: Srinivasa Ramanujan was born in 1887 in Erode, in southern India, into a poor Brahmin family. He encountered a second-hand book of mathematical results as a teenager and worked through it obsessively, deriving and extending everything in it. He was so absorbed that he failed his other subjects, lost his scholarship twice, and never completed a degree. He took a job as a shipping clerk in Madras and filled notebooks in his spare time.

What he produced was unlike ordinary mathematics. He wrote down results — infinite series, strange identities, formulas for counting — often with no proof at all, saying the ideas came to him, sometimes crediting the family goddess. Several were astonishingly accurate: one of his series for pi produces eight correct digits with every term, and is still used in software today.

In 1913 he posted a letter of these results to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy. Hardy's first reaction was that it must be a fraud, because the formulas were too strange to invent and too difficult to have come from nowhere. Then he worked through them and concluded they had to be genuine, since, as he put it, nobody could have the imagination to invent them falsely. He arranged for Ramanujan to come to England.

The five years that followed produced extraordinary work and considerable misery. Ramanujan was a strict vegetarian in wartime England, where food was rationed and suitable ingredients were scarce, and he was often cold, isolated and unwell. He returned to India in 1919 and died the following year, aged 32. His notebooks kept mathematicians busy for a century; a lost notebook rediscovered in 1976 contained results that turned out to matter in the study of black holes.
wow: Told that the number 1729 was dull, he replied instantly that it was the smallest number expressible as two cubes added together in two different ways.

quiz.q: How did Ramanujan learn mathematics?
What was unusual about his results?

title: Leonardo Finished Almost Nothing
hook: The most famous genius in history left most of his work unfinished.
story: Leonardo da Vinci was born in 1452 near Florence, the son of a notary and a peasant woman, unable to inherit his father's profession and given no formal education in Latin or mathematics. He taught himself, and later signed notes as a disciple of experience — a small dig at scholars who trusted books over observation.

His notebooks run to thousands of pages: flying machines, a diving suit, a parachute, gears, water pumps, studies of how blood swirls through a heart valve that were only confirmed correct in the twentieth century. He dissected around thirty human bodies to draw anatomy properly, at a time when that was difficult and unpleasant work.

But he abandoned constantly. Commissions were delivered years late or never. A giant bronze horse was never cast. A mural technique he invented for The Last Supper began flaking within his lifetime. Patrons complained bitterly. He would stop painting to study the way water moves, then stop that to design a bridge.

The notebooks were written in mirror writing, right to left, probably because he was left-handed and it kept the ink from smudging rather than for secrecy. They were scattered after his death and much was lost, which is why many of his ideas had no influence at all — others invented them independently centuries later.
wow: He wrote a job application letter to the Duke of Milan listing his military engineering skills, and mentioned painting almost as an afterthought at the end.

quiz.q: Why did he write in mirror writing?
a: Probably to stop smudging, being left-handed

quiz.q: What happened to most of his projects?

title: The Man Behind the Word Algorithm
hook: Two words you use in mathematics come from one scholar's name and one of his books.
story: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi worked in Baghdad in the early 800s, at a centre of learning where scholars gathered and translated texts from Greek, Persian and Indian sources. He wrote a book on solving equations whose title included the word al-jabr, meaning the restoring or completing of something. Translated into Latin, al-jabr became algebra.

His own name fared similarly. Latin writers rendered al-Khwarizmi as Algoritmi, and the word came to mean the step-by-step methods of calculation he described. Today an algorithm is any exact procedure a machine can follow — the foundation of every computer program.

The substance mattered more than the names. He set out general methods for solving whole classes of equations rather than tricks for individual problems, and explained them in ordinary words, aimed at people dealing with inheritance, trade and land — practical arithmetic for real disputes.

He also promoted the decimal number system with a symbol for zero, which had come from India. Europe was still using Roman numerals, which are miserable for calculation. Through his work and its translations, the digits we now call Arabic numerals spread west — and long multiplication, done on paper by any schoolchild, became possible.
wow: Try multiplying LVII by XXIII using only Roman numerals, and the importance of the change becomes obvious quickly.

quiz.q: Where does the word algebra come from?
a: Al-jabr, in the title of his book

quiz.q: What number system did he promote?

unknown: How much of the mathematics was his own is genuinely unclear. He worked in a house of translation where Greek, Persian and Indian texts arrived constantly, and scholars of the period often built on sources they named only loosely or not at all. Historians still argue over which parts of his algebra came from Babylonian methods, which from Indian work, and which he assembled himself — a problem made harder by how many manuscripts of the period are lost.

title: Nikola Tesla
hook: He won the argument about how to deliver electricity, and died with almost nothing.
story: Tesla arrived in America in 1884 with a few coins and a letter of introduction, and went to work for Thomas Edison. They fell out within a year. The dispute that followed was technical and enormous: Edison had built his business on direct current, which loses power badly over distance and needs a generating station every kilometre or so. Tesla believed in alternating current, which can be pushed to high voltage, sent far, then stepped back down.

Tesla's alternating-current motor and system, backed by the industrialist George Westinghouse, won. It is why a single power station can serve a whole region, and why the electricity in your wall is alternating current today.

He had other successes — radio-frequency work, remote control demonstrated in 1898 with a small boat that astonished onlookers, and fluorescent lighting — and a long run of expensive failures. A vast tower on Long Island, intended to transmit power without wires, was never finished and left him ruined.

He was a poor businessman among ruthless ones. He tore up a royalty agreement to help Westinghouse survive a financial crisis, a decision that would have made him extraordinarily rich. He spent his last years in a New York hotel, largely alone, feeding pigeons, and died in 1943 owing money.
wow: The unit of magnetic field strength is named the tesla, and the alternating-current system he designed still powers most of the world.

quiz.q: Why did alternating current win?
a: It can be sent long distances efficiently

quiz.q: What happened to his royalty agreement?
a: He tore it up to help Westinghouse

unknown: The wireless power tower remains the great open question about him. He claimed it could send electricity through the Earth itself to any point on the planet, and investors withdrew before it was finished. Modern physicists mostly judge the plan unworkable as described, since the energy would spread and dissipate. Wireless charging does exist today, but only over a few centimetres, and nothing resembling his global system has ever been demonstrated.

title: The Book That Started an Argument
hook: A marine biologist wrote about birds falling silent, and an industry tried to destroy her.
story: Rachel Carson was a biologist and a gifted writer whose books about the sea had already made her well known. In the late 1950s she began gathering evidence about pesticides, particularly DDT, which was being sprayed enthusiastically across farmland and towns after its success against disease-carrying insects in the war.

The problem was that it did not stay where it was sprayed and did not break down quickly. It accumulated in soil and water, then concentrated as it moved up the food chain: insects to small birds to birds of prey. Eagles and falcons laid eggs with shells too thin to survive being sat on, and populations collapsed.

Silent Spring appeared in 1962. Chemical companies spent heavily attacking it, and much of the attack was personal rather than scientific — she was called hysterical, unqualified, a spinster with no children who could not understand practical farming. She was also, at the time, dying of cancer, which she kept private so it could not be used against her argument.

A presidential committee reviewed the science and backed her. DDT was banned for agriculture in the United States in 1972, a decade after the book and eight years after her death, and bald eagle and peregrine numbers recovered. She never argued for banning all pesticides — only for evidence, restraint, and honesty about consequences.
wow: DDT is still used carefully in some countries against malaria-carrying mosquitoes, which is roughly the balanced position Carson herself argued for.

quiz.q: What did DDT do to birds of prey?
What did Carson actually argue for?
a: Evidence and restraint, not a total ban

title: She Planted Trees and It Became Politics
hook: Planting a tree sounds harmless. In Kenya in the 1970s it was treated as a threat.
story: Wangari Maathai grew up in rural Kenya, won a scholarship to study in the United States, and became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate. Returning home, she listened to rural women describing their problems: streams drying up, firewood impossible to find, soil washing away, food harder to grow.

Her answer in 1977 was simple to the point of seeming naive. Pay women a small amount for each tree seedling they raised and planted. The Green Belt Movement grew from that, and over the following decades tens of millions of trees were planted, mostly by women who had never been paid for work before.

It became political because the trees stood in the way of things. Forests were being cleared for the benefit of powerful people, and public parks were being handed to developers. Maathai opposed both. She was beaten by police, arrested repeatedly, and once occupied a park to stop a tower being built there — successfully. The government called her a threat to order.

She lived long enough to see the position reverse. Kenya's politics changed, she was elected to parliament, served as a deputy minister for the environment, and in 2004 became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize — awarded for linking environment, democracy and peace.
wow: The Nobel committee's reasoning was that you cannot have peace where resources are stripped away and people have no voice in it.

quiz.q: How did the Green Belt Movement work?
a: Women were paid for seedlings they raised

quiz.q: Why was tree planting political?
a: Powerful people profited from clearing land

title: The Fossil Hunter Nobody Would Credit
hook: She found creatures nobody knew had existed, and was not allowed to join the society that discussed them.
story: Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis on the English coast, into a poor family that collected fossils from the cliffs to sell to tourists. Her father died when she was eleven, leaving debts, and the fossil trade became how the family survived.

She was extraordinarily good at it. At around twelve she and her brother uncovered the first ichthyosaur skeleton to be properly recognised. She went on to find the first complete plesiosaur — so strange that a leading scientist initially declared it a fake — and the first pterosaur discovered outside Germany. She worked the cliffs in winter, when storms exposed new fossils and landslides were most likely; a landslide killed her dog while she was working.

Her finds forced an uncomfortable conclusion. These animals matched nothing alive. Extinction, still debated at the time, became very hard to deny, and the age of the Earth started to look far greater than anyone had assumed.

She was largely written out of it. Scientific papers describing her specimens often failed to name her. As a woman she could not join the Geological Society of London, or attend its meetings, or publish in its journal — while gentlemen who bought her fossils presented them as their own discoveries. She died at 47, and the society published an obituary, having never let her through the door.
wow: The tongue-twister about selling seashells by the seashore is widely believed to have been written about her.

quiz.q: What did her finds help establish?
Could she join the Geological Society?

title: The Man Who Fed a Billion People
hook: Most people have never heard of him, and he may have saved more lives than anyone.
story: In the 1940s Norman Borlaug, an American plant scientist, went to Mexico to work on wheat. The country was importing much of its food and losing crops to a fungal disease called rust. He spent years crossing thousands of plants by hand, hunting for varieties that resisted it.

He then did something unusual: he grew two generations a year by shuttling seed between two sites at different altitudes and seasons, halving the time an experiment took. Colleagues thought it wrong-headed. It also produced varieties that grew well in more than one climate, which turned out to matter enormously.

The breakthrough was short wheat. Traditional tall wheat given plenty of fertiliser grows heavy heads and falls over, ruining the harvest. Borlaug bred short, stiff-stemmed varieties that could carry a heavy head upright. Yields multiplied. Mexico became self-sufficient, and when famine loomed in India and Pakistan in the 1960s the same wheat, with new farming methods, turned the forecasts around.

He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. He was also, later, a critic of parts of what he had started — the heavy use of fertiliser and water, and the pressure on small farmers — and argued that feeding people was a delay, not a solution, unless population and farming practice were addressed too.
wow: Estimates of lives saved by the wheat he bred usually start at several hundred million and run to a billion.

quiz.q: Why did short wheat matter?
a: It could hold a heavy head without falling over

quiz.q: What did he do to speed up breeding?
a: Grew two generations a year in two places

unknown: What follows is unresolved. The wheat that ended famines also needed fertiliser, irrigation and machinery, which favoured larger farms, drained aquifers in parts of India, and pushed many smallholders out. Yields have since stopped climbing as quickly. Researchers are now trying to breed crops that need less water and less nitrogen rather than more, and there is no agreement on whether another leap of that size is possible or whether the gains have to come from waste, diet and distribution instead.
